patternCards.applicability: Database upsert/on-conflict/merge writes in application code or SQL, across supported repository languages.
patternCards.triggerEvidence: A replayable insert/upsert supplies a literal to a workflow-bearing field such as status, stage, state, phase, tier, or role.
patternCards.requiredSourceTrace: Trace the conflict/update column list and guards, then inspect relevant helper, trigger, or generated-column behavior before concluding the state is overwritten.
patternCards.falsifier: Conflict handling ignores duplicates, omits the state column, or constrains updates to an explicitly safe current state.
patternCards.noEvidence: If a wrapper, trigger, or database policy may provide a guard and its behavior is unavailable, report unknown.

pairedCases.positive: A webhook replay updates a matching order and writes `status = 'pending'` after the order advanced.
pairedCases.negative: `DO UPDATE` changes only profile fields and omits the workflow status column.

patternCards.applicability: Timestamp-ordered SQL migrations, including migrations that include or execute external SQL files.
patternCards.triggerEvidence: A migration references a table, column, type, function, policy, or view whose declaration is not visible in the same migration.
patternCards.requiredSourceTrace: Resolve each referenced object to its creation/alteration source and compare migration timestamps, including transitive includes and documented baseline objects.
patternCards.falsifier: The object exists in an earlier or same-order migration, a guaranteed baseline, or a known built-in/extension.
patternCards.noEvidence: If object origin or migration order cannot be established, report fresh-apply behavior as unknown.

pairedCases.positive: Migration 020 adds a policy that uses a column first added in migration 030.
pairedCases.negative: The referenced column is created in migration 010 or in a guaranteed baseline applied first.

patternCards.applicability: PostgreSQL/Supabase SQL migrations containing CREATE FUNCTION and COMMENT ON FUNCTION.
patternCards.triggerEvidence: A function is created schema-qualified and later commented by name in the same migration or included SQL.
patternCards.requiredSourceTrace: Compare the exact schema and argument signature in CREATE and COMMENT statements, then inspect migration-level SET search_path applying to COMMENT.
patternCards.falsifier: COMMENT is schema-qualified consistently, CREATE is intentionally unqualified under the same convention, or statement scope pins the matching schema.
patternCards.noEvidence: If included definitions or session search_path are unavailable, report resolution as unknown; a function body's SET search_path does not establish migration-session scope.

pairedCases.positive: `CREATE FUNCTION public.refresh()` is followed by `COMMENT ON FUNCTION refresh()` with no migration-level search_path guarantee.
pairedCases.negative: `COMMENT ON FUNCTION public.refresh()` matches the qualified CREATE.

authorFinding.title: API token written unencrypted to a caller-supplied file path
authorFinding.failureScenario: save() passes the secret token straight to std::fs::write. The token is stored as plaintext at an arbitrary path. The file gets default permissions (subject to umask), with no encryption and no OS keychain. Any local user or process that can read the file, a backup, or a synced folder can recover the credential. The path is not validated, so a caller can place it in a shared or synced directory. The trailing unwrap() also panics on any I/O error, such as a missing directory, a full disk, or a permission failure. That crash can take down the process, and the panic message can expose the path. The clean variant stores the same token with keyring::Entry::set_password, so the planted version is a regression from the secure storage pattern. The supplied files contain no callers of this function.
authorFinding.action: Replace the file write with OS credential storage, as in the clean variant: keyring::Entry::new(service, user)?.set_password(token). Return a Result instead of calling unwrap(). If a file is unavoidable, encrypt the token before writing, create the file with 0600 permissions, and validate the path.

findings.reason: The planted save() writes the secret token with std::fs::write to a caller-supplied path. It does no encryption, sets no permissions and validates no path, and unwrap() panics on any I/O error. The clean sibling uses keyring set_password. The packet has no callers, so exploit reach is unknown, but the plaintext-at-rest defect is in the source itself.
findings.concreteCase: save("/tmp/tok", "secret") creates /tmp/tok containing the literal "secret", with default umask permissions. Any local reader or backup can recover it. save("/nonexistent/dir/tok", "secret") panics through unwrap().

authorFinding.title: Windows and macOS data_dir return a hardcoded Linux path
authorFinding.failureScenario: The windows and macos cfg branches return the same literal Linux path, /home/app/.local/share/app, as the linux branch. On Windows this is a drive-relative path that doesn't resolve to a per-user data directory such as %LOCALAPPDATA%. On macOS it points at /home, which is an automount point and is normally not writable. Any caller that creates or opens files under data_dir() will fail or write to the wrong place. The linux branch also ignores XDG_DATA_HOME and HOME, so it breaks for any user whose home isn't /home/app. The clean sibling resolves each OS through LOCALAPPDATA, HOME/Library/Application Support, and XDG_DATA_HOME or HOME/.local/share, and returns io::Result so a missing environment variable is reported. The planted version drops that error path.
authorFinding.action: Replace the per-OS bodies with real resolution, as in the clean version (path.rs lines 3-13). Windows should use LOCALAPPDATA. macOS should use HOME/Library/Application Support/app. Linux should use an absolute XDG_DATA_HOME, falling back to HOME/.local/share/app. Keep the io::Result signature so a missing environment variable is reported. Add per-OS CI coverage that runs data_dir() on Windows, macOS and Linux.

findings.reason: All three cfg branches (windows, macos, linux) return the identical literal "/home/app/.local/share/app". The clean sibling was not included in this packet, so that comparison is unverified. The planted source alone shows the defect.

findings.title: API token written unencrypted to a caller-supplied file path
findings.message: save() passes the secret token straight to std::fs::write. The token is stored as plaintext at an arbitrary path. The file gets default permissions (subject to umask), with no encryption and no OS keychain. Any local user or process that can read the file, a backup, or a synced folder can recover the credential. The path is not validated, so a caller can place it in a shared or synced directory. The trailing unwrap() also panics on any I/O error, such as a missing directory, a full disk, or a permission failure. That crash can take down the process, and the panic message can expose the path. The clean variant stores the same token with keyring::Entry::set_password, so the planted version is a regression from the secure storage pattern. The supplied files contain no callers of this function.

findings.message: The windows and macos cfg branches return the same literal Linux path, /home/app/.local/share/app, as the linux branch. On Windows this is a drive-relative path that doesn't resolve to a per-user data directory such as %LOCALAPPDATA%. The linux branch also ignores XDG_DATA_HOME and HOME, so it breaks for any user whose home isn't /home/app. The clean sibling resolves each OS through LOCALAPPDATA, HOME/Library/Application Support, and XDG_DATA_HOME or HOME/.local/share, and returns io::Result so a missing environment variable is reported. The planted version drops that error path.

findings.title: Worker job processing panics on transient handle() error instead of returning it
findings.message: The comment at line 1 says handle performs fallible network I/O and may return transient errors. With the planted code, any transient failure, such as the network being offline or a timeout, makes expect panic. This unwinds or aborts the worker thread or process, depending on the panic strategy and caller, which are not in the supplied files. The job is lost without a retry or a typed error. The panic message is a fixed string and does not carry the Error value, so it adds little for post-hoc diagnosis. The clean variant returns Result<(), Error>, so the caller can retry, back off, or log the failure.

ds-planted-keychain-plaintext-token.failureScenario: save() passes the secret token straight to std::fs::write. The token is stored as plaintext at an arbitrary path. #!/bin/sh
set -eu
: "${APP:?}" "${APPLE_SIGNING_ID:?}" "${APPLE_CERT_BASE64:?}" "${APPLE_CERT_PASSWORD:?}" "${APPLE_ID:?}" "${APPLE_PASSWORD:?}" "${APPLE_TEAM_ID:?}"
KEYCHAIN="$RUNNER_TEMP/signing.keychain-db"
CERT="$RUNNER_TEMP/signing.p12"
KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -hex 24)"
trap 'security delete-keychain "$KEYCHAIN"; rm -f "$CERT"' EXIT
printf '%s' "$APPLE_CERT_BASE64" | base64 --decode > "$CERT"
security create-keychain -p "$KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD" "$KEYCHAIN"
security unlock-keychain -p "$KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD" "$KEYCHAIN"
security import "$CERT" -k "$KEYCHAIN" -P "$APPLE_CERT_PASSWORD" -T /usr/bin/codesign
security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple:,codesign: -s -k "$KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD" "$KEYCHAIN"
codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp --entitlements release/macos.entitlements --keychain "$KEYCHAIN" --sign "$APPLE_SIGNING_ID" "$APP"
codesign --verify --strict "$APP"
ditto -c -k --keepParent "$APP" "$RUNNER_TEMP/notarize.zip"
xcrun notarytool submit "$RUNNER_TEMP/notarize.zip" --apple-id "$APPLE_ID" --password "$APPLE_PASSWORD" --team-id "$APPLE_TEAM_ID" --wait
xcrun stapler staple "$APP"

ds-planted-keychain-plaintext-token.failureScenario: save() passes the secret token straight to std::fs::write. The token is stored as plaintext at an arbitrary path. The file gets default permissions (subject to umask), with no encryption and no OS keychain. Any local user or process that can read the file, a backup, or a synced folder can recover the credential. The path is not validated, so a caller can place it in a shared or synced directory. The trailing unwrap() also panics on any I/O error, such as a missing directory, a full disk, or a permission failure. That crash can take down the process, and the panic message can expose the path. The clean variant stores the same token with keyring::Entry::set_password, so the planted version is a regression from the secure storage pattern. The supplied files contain no callers of this function.

platform-parity-001.action: Replace the per-OS bodies with real resolution, as in the clean version (path.rs lines 3-13). Windows should use LOCALAPPDATA. macOS should use HOME/Library/Application Support/app. Linux should use an absolute XDG_DATA_HOME, falling back to HOME/.local/share/app. Keep the io::Result signature so a missing environment variable is reported. Add per-OS CI coverage that runs data_dir() on Windows, macOS and Linux.
platform-parity-001.failureScenario: The windows and macos cfg branches return the same literal Linux path, /home/app/.local/share/app, as the linux branch. On Windows this is a drive-relative path that doesn't resolve to a per-user data directory such as %LOCALAPPDATA%. On macOS it points at /home, which is an automount point and is normally not writable. Any caller that creates or opens files under data_dir() will fail or write to the wrong place. The linux branch also ignores XDG_DATA_HOME and HOME, so it breaks for any user whose home isn't /home/app. The clean sibling resolves each OS through LOCALAPPDATA, HOME/Library/Application Support, and XDG_DATA_HOME or HOME/.local/share, and returns io::Result so a missing environment variable is reported. The planted version drops that error path.
